summary.text: Theseus and Pirithous swore each to marry a daughter of Zeus — the Athenian hid the child Helen at Aphidnae and went down with his friend to fetch Persephone; Hades bound them on the Chair of Forgetfulness until Heracles raised Theseus alone, while the Dioscuri stormed Aphidnae and led Aethra away captive.
summary.citation: Apollod. 3.10.7, Epit. 1.23; Hyg. Fab. 79; Hom. Il. 3.144

chapters.title: The oath of the comrades
chapters.text: Theseus and Peirithous, son of Ixion and king of the Lapiths, bound themselves by oath: each would marry a daughter of Zeus. Theseus took Helen, still a child, and carried her off from Sparta; Peirithous would have Persephone herself — a vow that drove them both to the house of Hades.

chapters.title: Helen at Aphidnae
chapters.text: Theseus hid Helen and her brothers' future prize at Aphidnae in Attica, leaving his mother Aethra to guard the girl. While he and Pirithous descended, Castor and Polydeuces — Helen's divine brothers — marched against the fortress, recovered their sister, and took Aethra captive to serve her in Sparta until the Trojan War.
chapters.citation: Apollod. Epit. 1.23; Hom. Il. 3.144; Hyg. Fab. 79

chapters.title: The Chair of Forgetfulness
chapters.text: In the underworld Hades welcomed the pair with feigned hospitality and seated them on the Chair of Forgetfulness — or Stone of Unforgetting — from which they could not rise, while coils of serpents held them fast. Pirithous had come to steal the queen of the dead; the lord of the shades kept him bound for ever.

chapters.title: Heracles raises Theseus
chapters.text: When Heracles came down for Cerberus on his last labour, he found the trapped comrades and raised Theseus from the chair — though the earth quaked when he tried to free Pirithous, and the Lapith remained in Hades for his impiety. Theseus returned to find Helen gone, Aethra a captive, and Menestheus son of Peteos already seizing the throne of Athens.
